## Exercises  

### Exercise 1

Create a vector of three elements (2,4,6) and name that vector `vec_a`. Create a second vector, `vec_b`, that contains $(8,10,12)$. Add these two vectors together and name the result `vec_c`.

```{r}
vec_a <- c(2,4,6)
vec_b <- c(8,10,12)
vec_c <- c(vec_a + vec_b) #best practice would be to show the answer output and remove the c() notation. see the code chunk below
```

```{r} 
vec_a <- 2,4,6 #not quite sure how to remove the c notation without getting an error
vec_b <- 8,10,12
vec_c <- vec_a + vec_b
```

Here I made two vectors and added the vectors together using the add function.

### Exercise 2

Create a vector, named `vec_d`, that contains only two elements (14,20). Add this vector to `vec_a`. What is the result and what do you think R did (look up the recycling rule using Google)? What is the warning message that R gives you?

```{r}
vec_d <- c(14,20)
vec_e <- c(vec_d + vec_a)
```
The result is vec_e num [1:3] 16, 24, 20. Because these vectors are of different lengths, R recycled the shorter vector, vec_d. R recycled by adding 14 to the third value in vector a (which is 6), to output 20 as our third value in vec_e. We got a warning message warning us that the vectors were of different lengths.

### Exercise 3

Next add $5$ to the vector `vec_a`. What is the result and what did R do? Why doesn't in give you a warning message similar to what you saw in the previous problem?

```{r}
vec_a + 5 
```

Here there is no warning because we are just adding 5 to every value in the original vec_a. It created a hidden structure c(5,5,5) that would match the number of values in vec_a and be added to those values. 


### Exercise 5

Generate the vector of even numbers $\left\{ 2,4,6,\dots,20\right\}$

**a)** Using the `seq()` function and

```{r}
seq(from=2, to=20, by=2)
```

I created a sequence using the "from, to, by" format of even numbers from 2 to 20.

**b)** Using the a:b shortcut and some subsequent algebra. *Hint: Generate a sequence of integers then multiple by 2*.

```{r}
(1:10)*2
```
I used the a:b shortcut for 1 through 10 and multiplied by 2 to get the set of even integers from 2 to 20.

### Exercise 6

Generate a vector of $21$ elements that are evenly placed between $0$ and $1$ using the `seq()` command and name this vector `x`. 


```{r}
(x <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, by = 1/20)) #this is the same as using length.out = 21 
```

Here using the from, to, by notation I created a sequence from 0 to 1 with 21 values. I found that using the fraction 1/20 makes 21 values. If I used 1/21, that would create 22 values.


### Exercise 8

Generate the vector $\left\{ 2,2,2,2,4,4,4,4,8,8,8,8\right\}$ using the `rep()` command. You might need to check the help file for `rep()`. In particular, look at the optional argument `each=`.

```{r}
rep(c(2,4,8), each = 4) 
```

I concatenated the values 2,4,8 using each=4 in order to get 4 twos, then 4 fours, then 4 eights. Otherwise they would be alternating 2,4,8 etc.

### Exercise 11

Create and manipulate a data frame.

**a)** Create a `data.frame` named `my.trees` that has the following columns:

  + Girth = {8.3, 8.6, 8.8, 10.5, 10.7, 10.8, 11.0}
  + Height= {70, 65, 63, 72, 81, 83, 66}
  + Volume= {10.3, 10.3, 10.2, 16.4, 18.8, 19.7, 15.6}
  
```{r}
my.trees <- data.frame(
  Girth = c(8.3, 8.6, 8.8, 10.5, 10.7, 10.8, 11.0),
  Height = c(70, 65, 63, 72, 81, 83, 66),
  Volume = c(10.3, 10.3, 10.2, 16.4, 18.8, 19.7, 15.6))

my.trees
```

I created a data frame named my.trees with the values for Girth, Height, and Volume given.
  
Complete the following without using `dplyr` functions

**b)** Extract the third observation (i.e. the third row)

```{r}
my.trees[3,]
```
Using the square brackets, I selected the third row.

**c)** Extract the Girth column referring to it by name (don't use a numerical value based on column position).

```{r}
my.trees[ , "Girth"] 
```

Using the square brackets, we can insert the column name. We could also use my.trees$Girth, the dollar sign is what we use to reference a column by its label. 

**d)** Print out a data frame of all the observations *except* for the fourth observation. (i.e. Remove the fourth observation/row.)

```{r}
my.trees[-4, ]
```

By putting "-4" in the row, column notation, we eliminate the 4th observation (row).

**e)** Use the `which()` command to create a vector of row indices that have a `girth` greater than 10. Call that vector `index`.

```{r}
index <- which(my.trees$Girth > 10)
# could also do it this way, which(my.trees[ , "Girth"]>10)
index
```

This created a vector of row indices that have Girth greater than 10. Rows 4,5,6,7 have a girth greater than 10.

**f)** Use the `index` vector to create a small data set with just the large girth trees.

```{r}
large.girth.trees <- my.trees[index, ]
large.girth.trees
```
Here I used the index vector to create a small data set with just the large girth trees.

**g)** Use the `index` vector to create a small data set with just the small girth trees.

```{r}
index2 <- which(my.trees$Girth <= 10)
small.girth.trees <- my.trees[index2, ]
small.girth.trees #here we can use -index, instead of creating another index vector, index 2. see code chunk below 

```


```{r}
small.girth.trees <- my.trees[-index, ]
small.girth.trees
```


I created another index, this time index2, to display just the trees with a girth less than or equal to 10.

### Exercise 12 

The following code creates a `data.frame` and then has two different methods for removing the rows with `NA` values in the column `Grade`. Explain the difference between the two.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
df <- data.frame(name= c('Alice','Bob','Charlie','Daniel'),
                 Grade = c(6,8,NA,9))

df[ -which(  is.na(df$Grade) ), ]
df[  which( !is.na(df$Grade) ), ]
```

One way to remove rows with NA values is to add the "-" in front of the which. This negative will tell R to remove that element.Another way is to use a "!" which is used for negation. For any logical vector of values, the ! flips the logical values.

### Exercise 14 

Create and manipulate a list.

**a)** Create a list named my.test with elements

  + x = c(4,5,6,7,8,9,10)
  + y = c(34,35,41,40,45,47,51)
  + slope = 2.82
  + p.value = 0.000131
  
  
```{r}
x <- c(4,5,6,7,8,9,10)
y <- c(34,35,41,40,45,47,51)
slope <-  2.82
p.value <- 0.000131

my.test <- list(x=x, y=y, slope=slope, p.value=p.value)
str(my.test)
```
I created a list with the vectors x, y, slope, and p-value.

**b)** Extract the second element in the list.

```{r}
my.test$y ##here we can also use my.test[[2]] to pull it numerically 
```

I extracted the second element by using our $ notation.

**c)** Extract the element named `p.value` from the list.
```{r}
my.test$p.value
```

I extracted the p-value by using the same $ notation.
